gloss_terse: Wine; Aramaic term for fermented grape beverage, used in official decrees and royal banquet contexts.
gloss_readable: An Aramaic noun for wine, cognate with the Hebrew poetic term chemer. It appears in two distinct settings: Persian imperial decrees authorizing temple provisions (Ezra 6:9; 7:22) and the infamous banquet of Belshazzar where sacred vessels were profaned (Dan 5:1, 2, 4, 23). The Syriac cognate confirms the basic meaning. That this single word bridges solemn administrative grants and reckless royal feasting captures wine's dual role in the ancient Near East -- a staple of sustenance and a catalyst for hubris.

senses.1: Wine as a fermented grape beverage. All six occurrences divide between Persian royal provisions for the Jerusalem temple (Ezra 6:9; 7:22, absolute form chamar) and the vessels of wine at Belshazzar's feast (Dan 5:1, 2, 4, 23, emphatic form chamra). The consistent rendering across languages -- Spanish 'vino,' German 'Wein,' English 'wine' -- confirms a single straightforward sense with no semantic branching.

gloss_terse: The stork; a large migratory wading bird, named from the root meaning 'faithful, loyal' for its devoted parenting.
gloss_readable: The feminine noun chasidah designates the stork, etymologically derived from chesed ('loyal love'), reflecting ancient observation of the bird's devoted care for its young -- a connection the Latin name pietaticultrix also captures. Listed among unclean birds in the dietary laws (Lev 11:19; Deut 14:18), the stork appears as a creature of reliable seasonal migration in Jeremiah 8:7 -- shaming Israel who fails to 'know the appointed times.' In Psalm 104:17 it nests in the fir trees, and in Zechariah 5:9 two women with stork-like wings carry the ephah of wickedness away.

senses.1: The stork, a large migratory wading bird classified as ritually unclean (Lev 11:19; Deut 14:18). Spanish 'cigueña' and English 'stork' converge on a single zoological referent. The bird's association with parental devotion (from the root ch-s-d, 'loyalty') makes Jeremiah's irony pointed: even the stork knows its seasons, but God's people do not know his ordinances (Jer 8:7). In Ps 104:17 it inhabits the treetops; in Zech 5:9 its broad wings become a prophetic image.

gloss_terse: A species of locust (collective), consistently associated with devastating agricultural destruction and divine judgment.
gloss_readable: The masculine noun chasil refers to a specific type of locust, always collective and always destructive. It appears exclusively in contexts of agricultural plague and divine judgment -- the locust swarms of Joel 1:4 and 2:25, the covenant curses of 1 Kings 8:37 and 2 Chronicles 6:28, and the gathering of spoil 'like the gathering of the chasil' in Isaiah 33:4. The exact species remains debated, but the word consistently parallels arbeh (the common locust) and yeleq (the creeping locust), suggesting a particular stage or variety within the locust family.

senses.1: A destructive species or stage of locust, always appearing as an agent of crop devastation. Spanish renders it variously as 'saltamontes' (grasshopper) and 'destructor' (destroyer), while English traditions waver between 'caterpillar' and 'destroying locust.' The word always parallels other locust terms -- arbeh and yeleq in Joel 1:4; 2:25, and arbeh alone in 1 Kgs 8:37 and Ps 78:46. Isaiah 33:4 uses its swarming and gathering behavior as a simile for the plundering of Assyria's spoil.

gloss_terse: The cupped hollow of the hands; always dual, denoting both hands together as a vessel for holding or scooping.
gloss_readable: The noun chophen appears only in the dual form chophnayim, picturing two cupped hands held together as a natural vessel. Moses and Aaron fill their chophnayim with soot to fling toward heaven, triggering boils on Egypt (Exod 9:8). The high priest takes a chophnayim-full of incense into the Holy of Holies on the Day of Atonement (Lev 16:12). Agur's riddle asks who has gathered the wind in his fists (Prov 30:4), and Qoheleth declares that one handful with quietness surpasses two handfuls with toil (Eccl 4:6). The Aramaic and Ethiopic cognates confirm the concrete image of cupped palms.

senses.1: The hollow formed by two cupped hands together, always in dual form (chophnayim), used as a measure or container for grasping and holding material. Spanish 'puños' (fists) and English 'handfuls/fists' capture the concrete bodily image. In Exod 9:8 it holds furnace soot; in Lev 16:12 burning incense coals; in Prov 30:4 it is an impossible container for the wind; in Eccl 4:6 it measures the contrast between contentment and anxious toil. Ezekiel 10:2, 7 extends the image to the cherub's hands filling with coals.

gloss_terse: Hazeroth; a wilderness encampment of Israel during the exodus, meaning 'enclosures' or 'courtyards.'
gloss_readable: Chatseroth is a proper place name designating one of Israel's wilderness encampments after leaving Sinai. The name derives from chatser ('enclosure, courtyard'), perhaps suggesting a site with natural rock enclosures or settled compounds. It is remembered especially as the location where Miriam and Aaron challenged Moses's authority and Miriam was struck with skin disease (Num 12). The itinerary notices in Numbers 11:35, 33:17-18 record arrival and departure, while Deuteronomy 1:1 lists it among landmarks framing Moses's final address.

senses.1: The proper place name Hazeroth (chatseroth), a wilderness station on Israel's exodus route between Kibroth-hattaavah and the wilderness of Paran. Multilingual renderings are uniformly transliterated -- 'Hazeroth' in English, Spanish 'Hazerot,' French and German 'Hazeroth' -- confirming a single geographic referent. The site is best known as the setting for Miriam's rebellion against Moses (Num 12:1-16). Its listing in Deut 1:1 among geographic markers suggests it was a recognized landmark in Transjordan traditions.

gloss_terse: Waste, desolate, ruined; describing cities or places that have been destroyed and left uninhabited.
gloss_readable: The adjective charev (II) describes places -- especially cities and buildings -- that lie in a state of ruin and desolation, devoid of inhabitants. It differs from the related verb charav ('to be dry, desolate') by functioning as a fixed descriptor of post-destruction states. Nehemiah uses it twice of Jerusalem's burned gates and broken walls (Neh 2:3, 17). Ezekiel employs it in restoration oracles where the formerly desolate cities will be rebuilt and inhabited (Ezek 36:35, 38). Haggai applies it pointedly to the temple lying in ruins while the people live in paneled houses (Hag 1:4, 9).

senses.1: In a state of ruin, waste, or desolation, used of cities, buildings, and inhabited places that have been destroyed or left without people. Spanish consistently renders 'desolada/desolado,' while English gives 'desolate' and 'ruined.' The prophetic texts use this adjective to create powerful contrasts: Jeremiah's 'desolate, without man or beast' (Jer 33:10, 12), Ezekiel's vision of ruined cities becoming like the garden of Eden (Ezek 36:35), and Haggai's rebuke that God's house lies charev while the people's own houses are finished (Hag 1:4, 9).

gloss_terse: Trembling, fearful; one who quakes from terror in battle or from reverent awe before God's word.
gloss_readable: The verbal adjective chared describes a person in a state of trembling, whether from battlefield terror or from reverent awe before God. Gideon's famous reduction of his army begins by sending home every chared -- everyone trembling with fear (Judg 7:3). Eli's heart trembles for the ark of God (1 Sam 4:13). But in Ezra and Isaiah, the word takes on a profoundly positive meaning: those who 'tremble at God's word' are the faithful remnant, the devout who take divine revelation seriously (Ezra 9:4; 10:3; Isa 66:2, 5).

senses.1: Trembling, fearful, or awe-struck -- a verbal adjective covering both physical trembling from fear and reverent trembling before God. Spanish distinguishes 'temblando' (trembling) from 'los que tembláis' (you who tremble), capturing the range. In Judg 7:3 it parallels 'afraid' (yare) as grounds for military dismissal. In 1 Sam 4:13 Eli's heart trembles with anxiety for the ark. The Ezra-Isaiah usage (Ezra 9:4; 10:3; Isa 66:2, 5) transforms trembling into a mark of spiritual devotion -- those who chared at God's commandments are his true servants.

gloss_terse: Gold, fine gold; a poetic synonym for zahav used in wisdom literature to express supreme material value.
gloss_readable: The noun charutz (V) is a poetic term for gold, distinct from the common zahav and the Aramaic dehav. It appears exclusively in elevated poetic contexts -- Wisdom literature and Psalms -- always paired with silver (keseph) to frame comparisons of supreme value. Proverbs repeatedly declares that wisdom surpasses charutz (Prov 3:14; 8:10, 19; 16:16). The Psalmist pictures dove wings shimmering with yellow-green charutz (Ps 68:14), and Zechariah describes Tyre heaping up gold like dust (Zech 9:3). The Phoenician cognate charuts confirms the precious-metal meaning.

senses.1: Precious refined gold, used as a poetic synonym for zahav exclusively in elevated literary contexts. German 'Gold' and 'Feingold,' Spanish 'oro,' and English 'gold' all converge, though French curiously shows some confusion with other senses of the root charats ('diligent, sharp'). Always paralleled with silver (keseph), charutz serves as the standard of highest earthly value that wisdom nonetheless surpasses (Prov 3:14; 8:10, 19; 16:16). In Ps 68:13-14 it colors the shimmering wings of a dove; in Zech 9:3 it pictures Tyre's accumulated wealth.

gloss_terse: Burning heat of anger, fierce wrath; always in the construct phrase chori aph ('burning of nostril/anger').
gloss_readable: The masculine noun chori means 'burning' or 'fierce heat' and appears exclusively in the fixed construct phrase chori (ha-)aph -- literally 'burning of the nostril,' meaning fierce anger or hot wrath. It intensifies the already vivid Hebrew image of anger as heat in the nose. Moses departs Pharaoh in great chori aph (Exod 11:8). Jonathan rises from the table in chori aph over his father's shaming of David (1 Sam 20:34). The phrase also describes divine wrath (Deut 29:24) and the anger of armies and kings (2 Chr 25:10; Isa 7:4; Lam 2:3).

senses.1: The burning heat or fierceness of anger, exclusively in the construct phrase chori aph ('burning of anger'). Spanish 'ardor de' (burning of) and English 'burning of' preserve the construct relationship faithfully. The word intensifies aph ('anger, nostril') by adding the image of fire or extreme heat. It describes Moses's fury at Pharaoh (Exod 11:8), Jonathan's outrage for David (1 Sam 20:34), God's wrath on the land (Deut 29:24), Ephraimite soldiers' anger at dismissal (2 Chr 25:10), and the 'burning anger' of Rezin and Pekah that Isaiah tells Ahaz not to fear (Isa 7:4).

gloss_terse: Horite; the pre-Edomite cave-dwelling inhabitants of the hill country of Seir, displaced by Esau's descendants.
gloss_readable: The gentilic noun chori (II) designates the Horites, the indigenous people of the Seir hill country before the Edomites displaced them. The name likely derives from chor ('cave'), marking them as cave-dwellers -- fitting the terrain of Edom's sandstone cliffs. Genesis 14:6 places them in their mountains at the time of the eastern kings' invasion. Genesis 36:20-30 provides a detailed genealogy of Seir the Horite and his descendants. Deuteronomy 2:12, 22 records their displacement by the sons of Esau as a paradigm for how God gives nations their territories.

senses.1: The Horites, a pre-Edomite ethnic group inhabiting the hill country of Seir, always with the article (ha-chori). Spanish 'el horeo / los horeos,' German 'der Horite / der Choriter,' and English 'the Horite / the Horites' uniformly transliterate. The name probably means 'cave-dweller' (from chor, 'cave'), appropriate to Edom's sandstone geography. Genesis 36:20 identifies 'Seir the Horite' as the ancestral figure; Gen 14:6 locates them in their mountains; Deut 2:12, 22 narrates their dispossession by Esau's descendants as theological precedent for Israel's own territorial inheritance.
